claim: 324 mitochondria were identified within 63 dendritic segments from 4 cells collected from 2 animals in the dataset.
source: From these 3D annotations, we first characterized the basic structure and organization of postsynaptic mitochondria in our dataset (n=324 mitochondria identified within 63 dendritic segments from 4 cells collected from 2 animals).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the sample size and composition of the dataset used for characterizing postsynaptic mitochondria.

claim: The median inter-mitochondrion distance in basal dendrites is 3.025 µm with an IQR of 5.281 µm.
source: Mitochondria were distributed throughout dendrites, with infrequent, large (>10 µm) gaps between individual mitochondria (median inter-mitochondrion distance = 3.025 µm, IQR = 5.281 µm, Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative measurements of inter-mitochondrion distance and references Figure 1A and B showing the distribution.

claim: Mitochondria in basal dendrites of ferret layer 2/3 cortical cells have a median volume of 0.248 µm³ with an IQR of 0.443 µm³.
source: Mitochondria in the basal dendrites of ferret layer 2/3 cortical cells were typically small (median volume = 0.248 µm3, IQR = 0.443 µm3, surface area = 2.537 µm2, IQR = 3.144 µm2, Figure 1D–E), with a short length through the dendrite (maximum length median = 1.137 µm, IQR = 0.881 µm, Figure 1F), in comparison to many in vitro and in vivo reports of mouse cortical neurons (Lewis et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative measurements of mitochondrial volume with statistical descriptors and references supporting figures.

claim: 4.9% of dendritic spines (10 out of 203 spines) contain mitochondria positioned in the spine neck or head.

claim: Of spines containing mitochondria, 2 out of 10 had mitochondria entirely within the spine head, 5 out of 10 at the junction between head and neck, and 3 out of 10 within the neck.

evidence: The manuscript provides correlation statistics between mitochondrial volume at 1 µm radius and spine-soma distance.

claim: Mitochondria volume within 5 µm radius is not correlated with spine-soma distance (r=0.104, p=0.129, n=121).
source: While this relationship was not observed for mitochondria within a 5 µm radius (5 µm: r=0.104, p=0.129, n=121 spines; Figure 2J), there is a simple explanation: the volume fraction of dendrite occupied by mitochondria increases with distance from the soma (Turner et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript provides correlation statistics between mitochondrial volume at 5 µm radius and spine-soma distance, along with a citation explaining the observation.

claim: The volume fraction of dendrite occupied by mitochondria increases with distance from the soma.
source: While this relationship was not observed for mitochondria within a 5 µm radius (5 µm: r=0.104, p=0.129, n=121 spines; Figure 2J), there is a simple explanation: the volume fraction of dendrite occupied by mitochondria increases with distance from the soma (Turner et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript cites a published study to support this claim about mitochondrial distribution.

claim: 148 out of 164 spines were tuned (selectivity >0.1).
source: For each tuned spine (selectivity >0.1, n=148/164 spines; see Methods), we calculated orientation preference and compared this value to the orientation tuning of each parent soma (∆ϴpref; see Methods).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts of tuned spines in the dataset.

claim: Each of the four cells in the dataset had orientation selectivity ranging from 0.40 to 0.57, with a mean of 0.46 ± 0.08 s.d.
source: Each of the four cells in our dataset was similarly tuned for orientation (selectivity range = 0.40–0.57, mean = 0.46 ± 0.08 s.d.).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific measurements of orientation selectivity for the cells in the dataset.

claim: Mitochondrial volume within a 1 µm radius is correlated with difference in orientation preference relative to the soma (bootstrapped Spearman's r=0.315 ± 0.11 s.e.m., p=0.010, n=54).
source: We found that mitochondrial volume within a 1 µm radius was correlated with difference in orientation preference relative to the soma (bootstrapped spearman's r=0.315 ± 0.11 s.e.m., p=0.010, n=54 spines; Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript provides correlation statistics between mitochondrial volume at 1 µm radius and spine-soma orientation preference difference.

claim: Co-tuned spines (∆ϴpref <22.5°) and differentially tuned spines (∆ϴpref >67.5°) do not differ in selectivity (p=0.12) or max response amplitude (p=0.58).
source: This relationship could not be attributed to different properties of co-tuned (∆ϴpref <22.5°, n=68) and differentially tuned spines (∆ϴpref >67.5°, n=30) (selectivity: p=0.12, max response amplitude: p=0.58).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical comparisons between co-tuned and differentially tuned spines for selectivity and response amplitude.

claim: The trend of mitochondrial volume correlating with orientation preference difference was found for all four cells examined (1 µm: mean Spearman's r=0.49 ± 0.22 s.d.; 5 µm: mean Spearman's r=0.09 ± 0.13 s.d.).

claim: Within dendritic segments with greater mitochondrial volume at 5 µm radius, calcium is quickly removed from spines and cytoplasm.
source: This weak relationship suggests that within some dendritic segments, a greater volume of mitochondria leads to rapid removal of calcium out of the spine and cytoplasm, in agreement with a recent modeling study (Leung et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript infers this mechanism from the observed weak correlation and cites a modeling study supporting this interpretation.

claim: Local heterogeneity in orientation preference is strongly correlated with mitochondria volume within a 1 µm radius (r=0.563, p=0.0005, n=31).
source: Similar to spine-soma difference in orientation preference, we found that local heterogeneity was strongly correlated with mitochondria volume within a 1 µm radius (r=0.563, p=0.0005, n=31 spines; Figure 4B), and not within 5 µm (r=0.017, p=0.432, n=107 spines; Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript provides correlation statistics between local heterogeneity and mitochondrial volume at 1 µm radius.

claim: Local heterogeneity in orientation preference is not correlated with mitochondria volume within 5 µm radius (r=0.017, p=0.432, n=107).

evidence: The manuscript provides correlation statistics between local heterogeneity and mitochondrial volume at 5 µm radius.

claim: Local heterogeneity is correlated with spine co-tuning (circular r=0.33, p=0.0024, n=100).
source: Importantly, while local heterogeneity was correlated with spine co-tuning (circular r=0.33, p=0.0024, n=100 spines), this correlation was entirely due to inputs that closely matched the somatic preference.
evidence: The manuscript provides correlation statistics between local heterogeneity and spine co-tuning.

claim: The correlation between local heterogeneity and spine co-tuning is entirely due to inputs that closely matched the somatic preference.
source: Importantly, while local heterogeneity was correlated with spine co-tuning (circular r=0.33, p=0.0024, n=100 spines), this correlation was entirely due to inputs that closely matched the somatic preference.

claim: For differentially tuned spines (∆ϴpref >11.25°), local heterogeneity is still strongly correlated with mitochondria volume within 1 µm (Spearman's r=0.52, p=0.0052, n=50).
source: Focusing on these spines, local heterogeneity was still strongly correlated with mitochondria volume within 1 µm (Spearman's r=0.52, p=0.0052, n=50).

evidence: The manuscript provides correlation statistics between local average calcium activity and mitochondrial volume at 5 µm radius.

claim: In dendritic regions with particularly large volume of mitochondria, calcium is quickly buffered and calcium activity is attenuated within dendritic spines.
source: As this correlation was only observed at an extended radius, it suggests that dendritic regions with a particularly large volume of mitochondria, calcium is quickly buffered and calcium activity is attenuated within dendritic spines.
evidence: The manuscript infers this mechanism from the observed negative correlation at 5 µm radius.

claim: Spines with a mitochondrion in the head or neck have significantly larger spine head volume (median = 0.608 µm³, n=10) compared to spines without (median = 0.311 µm³, n=157, p=0.0014).
source: Spines with a mitochondrion in the head or neck had a significantly larger spine head volume compared to the majority of spines that do not (mito+: median = 0.608 µm3, n=10 spines; mito–: median = 0.311 µm3, n=157 spines, p=0.0014, Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.01, permutation test; Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical comparison of spine head volumes between spines with and without mitochondria.

claim: PSD area shows a non-significant trend toward being larger in spines with mitochondria (median = 0.396 µm², n=10) compared to those without (median = 0.244 µm², n=157, p=0.087).
source: A similar trend was observed for PSD area, but it was not significant (mito+: median = 0.396 µm2, n=10 spines; mito–: median = 0.244 µm2, n=157 spines, p=0.087, Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.12, permutation test; Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical comparison of PSD areas between spines with and without mitochondria.

claim: Spine neck length does not differ between spines with mitochondria (median = 1.850 µm, n=10) and those without (median = 1.65 µm, n=157, p=0.382).
source: Other anatomical properties such as spine neck length (mito+: median = 1.850 µm, n=10 spines; mito–: median = 1.65 µm, n=157 spines, p=0.382, Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.14, permutation test; Figure 5C) and distance of the spine from the soma (mito+: median = 52.32 µm, n=10 spines; mito–: median = 50.56 µm, n=157 spines, p=0.898, Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.42, permutation test; Figure 5D) showed no difference between spine groups.
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical comparison of spine neck lengths between spines with and without mitochondria.

claim: Distance from soma does not differ between spines with mitochondria (median = 52.32 µm, n=10) and those without (median = 50.56 µm, n=157, p=0.898).
source: Other anatomical properties such as spine neck length (mito+: median = 1.850 µm, n=10 spines; mito–: median = 1.65 µm, n=157 spines, p=0.382, Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.14, permutation test; Figure 5C) and distance of the spine from the soma (mito+: median = 52.32 µm, n=10 spines; mito–: median = 50.56 µm, n=157 spines, p=0.898, Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.42, permutation test; Figure 5D) showed no difference between spine groups.
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical comparison of spine-soma distances between spines with and without mitochondria.

claim: Spines with a mitochondrion in the head or neck are more selective for oriented gratings (median = 0.396, n=10) compared to spines without (median = 0.268, n=161, p=0.016).
source: Comparing other functional response properties, we found only a single metric showing a significant difference: orientation tuning selectivity. Spines with a mitochondrion were more selective for oriented gratings (mito+: median = 0.396, n=10 spines; mito–: median = 0.268, n=161 spines, p=0.016, Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.03, permutation test; Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical comparison of orientation selectivity between spines with and without mitochondria.

claim: Spine-soma difference of orientation preference does not differ between spines with mitochondria (median = 10.62, n=10) and those without (median = 30.17, n=146, p=0.451).
source: Unlike for dendritic mitochondria, we saw no difference in spine-soma difference of orientation preference (mito+: median = 10.62, n=10 spines; mito–: median = 30.17, p=0.451, n=146 spines, Mann-Whitney U test, p=0.23, permutation test; Figure 6B).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical comparison of spine-soma orientation preference difference between spines with and without mitochondria.

claim: Mitochondria positioned within dendritic spines may serve a different purpose than those within dendrites, supporting stronger synaptic inputs.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that mitochondria positioned within dendritic spines may serve a different purpose than those within the dendrites, supporting stronger synaptic inputs, which have been shown to be more selective for features of visual stimuli (Scholl et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript infers this interpretation from the observed differences in spine properties with and without mitochondria, citing a previous study.

claim: Postsynaptic mitochondria are critical for the development, plasticity, and maintenance of synaptic inputs.
